en: The Refutation of the Whole;
Homage to the Lord of the World; Homage to Samantabhadra.
No such excellence of practice has been cultivated by me, nor has such sacred learning been acquired;
yet, though I am fickle, I now desire to compose this mere fragment of meaning.
Having considered all this, let the wise examine what has been spoken here.
For generally, the activities of an infant please the minds of their parents;
however, that which possesses contradictory attributes cannot be a single entity.

Just as an object such as a jar possesses the superimposition of contradictory properties, so too does an object such as a gross blue thing; this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Here, the subject (*dharmin*) is the gross blue object being perceived.
And that [object], being established by experience and remaining uncontradicted, is proven by perception; it destroys the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) of the reason.

[Objection: But surely you yourselves maintain that the composite whole (*avayavin*) is non-existent; how then can it be established by perception? [Response: We do not accept the composite whole here as the subject (*dharmin*), but rather the object appearing as something gross, blue, and so forth.
In that case, the oneness of the whole (*avayavin*) would not be refuted by the conjunction of contradictory properties; yet it has been refuted.

If this is so, then what is your "whole"? If you say it is an object inherent (*samaveta*) in many parts and yet one, is that [object] different from or non-different from the coarse blue and so forth that appear? It cannot first be different, because it is admitted to be perceptible.
And nothing else appears apart from the manifest object that is gross and blue;
if it is not other [than that], then when its unity has been rejected, how can the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) remain unrefuted?
But surely, if the appearing object is not a substratum (*dharmin*) in the form of a whole, what then will be its well-established, undifferentiated nature? It is said in reply:
The coarse blue form appearing [in cognition] remains as a form established by direct perception even if the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted;
nor should it be thought that,
for those who maintain the theory of an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃcaya*), there exists any object in the form of a coarse shape that could serve as a well-known subject (*dharmin*).

For even if the composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, who has prevented the acceptance of a gross object consisting of multiple partless entities? It might be thought: "How could partless atoms appear in perception with a gross form, given the contradiction between the gross and the subtle? That too is not tenable; for it is precisely the atoms themselves, arising while excluding the space occupied by others and appearing in conjunction with one another, that manifest as having spatial extension.

Regarding the statement that "grossness" consists in occupying an extended space, and the claim that there is a contradiction between the gross and the subtle: do you intend to assert that the production of partless entities involves the exclusion of the spatial location of others, or that it is non-contradictory for such entities to appear together in a single cognition? Or do you consider this to be contradictory?

If this is not contradictory, then why is the gross form (*sthūlākāra*) contradictory? Therefore, when many partless [atoms] appear in a single cognition, the gross form—which exists at the time of appearance as a property of that appearance—is not real, because it does not exist in each [atom] individually. If you argue that it is therefore not "gross" before or after the appearance—no, for even then the capacity for appearance is possible;
for it is precisely when they are accumulated that atoms become capable of appearing.
And if they are gross when they are capable of appearing,
then there is a contradiction;
for one might say that when many partless entities appear, they must necessarily appear even without [any intervening space].

If there were no manifestation of the intervals between them, they would not appear as mutually distinct; and if the distinct intervals were not manifested, even a mere atom would become a solid mass,
yet we do not perceive any interval appearing between them.
Therefore, this [object], being continuous and a single gross entity, cannot consist of multiple partless atoms; rather, it must be a single entity whose very nature is grossness.
This too must be explained as follows:

is there an interval consisting of another atom of a different kind, or is it a connection with empty space? Among these, a connection with empty space, being a non-entity, cannot be an object of sensory perception; for in that which arises through the causal capacity of an object, it is only the object itself that can appear.

But how could an object of a different class, which is perceivable by another sense organ, appear in the cognition of a different sense organ, since it is not its object? We do not know by what other means it could possibly appear there.

As for the further argument that "if the intervening space were not perceived, the objects would not appear as distinct," in that case too, one must consider whether their "intervening space" is their mutual distinction (*viveka*) or their being devoid of the form of the other (*pararūpa-śūnyatā*).
Upon investigation, however, we perceive the isolation (*viveka*) of things as being precisely their emptiness of other-natures (*pararūpa-śūnyatā*).
For how could these appearing entities, which are empty of other-natures, not manifest as isolated?
But surely, the gross form does not belong to individual atoms; therefore, it must be admitted that it belongs to them when they are aggregated.

And just as the yellow form, which is impossible for each individual blue atom, is not seen even when many are present, so too, how could a gross form—which is impossible for each individual [atom]—exist in many? To this it has been said: a gross form is not contradictory to partless atoms, whereas a yellow form is indeed contradictory to blue.

In that case, even if there were many [atoms] possessing a blue form that is incompatible with yellow, how could there be a yellow form? It is not so; for the gross form is not incompatible with partlessness, according to the reasoning already stated.
Thus, it is established that the gross object, proven by direct perception, is the subject (*dharmin*) in this context.

This being the established case regarding the subject (*dharmin*), once it has been determined whether the reason (*hetu*) exists or does not exist therein, how could a gross object—which is simultaneously perceived as having both a moving and a non-moving form when a single part such as a hand is moving—not possess the conjunction of contradictory properties? For between the two forms—the moving and the non-moving—there is a contradiction based on their mutual exclusion;

for contradiction consists in the nature of mutual exclusion only between existence and non-existence, whereas between two real entities, it occurs precisely through their mutual exclusion of one another.
And here, while perception itself, by apprehending form as both mobile and immobile, establishes mutual exclusion through its own efficacy,
it is non-apprehension without qualification that brings about conventional usage;
such being the case:
It might be argued as follows:
when one part, such as the hand, is moving, the movement of the whole (the body) should not be admitted.

For at that time, it is only the part (*avayava*) that is seen to possess action, and one should not think: "Since the part possesses action, the whole (*avayavin*) which resides in it must also possess action, just as when a chariot moves, the person mounted upon it also moves.
This is because the causes for the actions of the part and the whole are distinct, and because those causes do not arise simultaneously.
For when there arises in the self the desire to shake the hand, then effort [arises]; then, from the conjunction of the self and the hand possessing that effort, motion occurs in the hand.

But when a specific effort for the purpose of shaking the body arises in the self, then, from the conjunction of the self and the body possessing that effort, action occurs in the body; such is the difference in the efficient cause (*nimitta*).

Therefore, when two things have distinct causes, how could the other—which has its birth dependent on a different cause—be produced in that same manner in the absence of that [specific] cause? As for the actions of the chariot and the person mounted upon it, although there is a difference in their causes, they occur simultaneously because their causes are co-existent.

Thus, regarding those two: impulsion (*nodana*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the action of the chariot, whereas the conjunction with the impeller (*nodyasaṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause of the action of the person mounted upon it.
And because those two exist simultaneously, the two actions also arise at once;

having considered all this, the Venerable Dharmottara stated: "In this case, no single part possesses action, for it is among the parts that the entity of action—namely, disjunction—is produced, since action is the independent cause with respect to the initiation of disjunction."
And when that conjunction, acting as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), is removed, the composite substance would cease to exist; thus it ceases.

Regarding this, the disciples of Kaṇāda say: A specific kind of action produced by pushing or striking is observed to originate a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction that initiates a substance.
But the other [type of action] initiates mere disjunction, yet not with the aforementioned specific quality; for,
as in the case of other actions such as the closing and opening of a lotus, no cessation of conjunction of parts is observed,
and likewise, even an action produced by effort lacks the capacity to bring about the cessation of conjunction.
Therefore, there is no cessation of the substance;
or rather, because of the non-obstruction [of its activity],
this is the resolution here.
In this case, if the whole possesses action, it must necessarily follow that its parts also possess action;
otherwise, there would be disjunction from the points of space occupied by the parts for the active whole, while there would be conjunction with points of space not occupied by the parts.
However, if the parts were devoid of action, they would not move away from the previously occupied regions of space.
Furthermore, the parts would not be connected with those regions occupied by the whole;

nor should the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts be said to result from the conjunctions and disjunctions of the whole, because it is not accepted that the conjunctions and disjunctions of the effect serve as the instrumental causes for the conjunctions and disjunctions of the cause—
it is rather the conjunctions and disjunctions of the cause alone that originate the conjunctions and disjunctions of the effect.
Nor can the opposite be maintained, for that would entail the abandonment of one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Since the parts and the whole would then occupy different locations, the relationship of supported and supporter (*ādhāryādhārabhāva*) would be lost, and consequently, even inherence (*samavāya*) could not be established.
Therefore, even if they are unwilling, the Vaiśeṣikas must accept this: when the whole possesses motion, the parts also possess motion.

Just as the parts possess motion when the whole possesses motion, so too, when the parts possess motion, their own parts must likewise possess motion; by this reasoning, one should understand that when the dyad (dvyaṇuka) possesses motion, the two atoms that compose it must also possess motion.
Therefore, the atoms connected to moving parts are themselves moving.

If, however, the atoms were inactive while being connected to inactive parts, then even the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) substance produced from them would necessarily be active when the atom is active; for the activity of every part is invariably concomitant with the activity of the whole. If it is argued that "the activity belongs to one atom and not to the other," then those two atoms—one active and one inactive—would be separated from each other, thereby abandoning the conjunction that initiates the substance.

Consequently, there would be the destruction of the substance itself; and thus, if the dyad-substance possessed motion, motion would also occur in the triad-substance. By this sequence, even a part that is observed to be stationary would become mobile. Therefore, atoms related to motionless parts would be motionless, whereas those being separated from mobile parts would possess the destruction of the conjunctions that originate the substance.

For an atom is partless; having traversed a spatial point of the sky measuring only a single atom, it joins with another atom. Then, when it is being divided [from that other], how could it remain without abandoning its proximity to that other atom? For an entity possessing parts, while joined with one object by means of one part, may traverse to another location by means of its other moving parts, thereby vacating the previously occupied points of space. But in the case of partless entities, this process is utterly impossible; thus, we perceive the logical consequence of the destruction of the substance itself.
Or rather, this conjunction of contradictory properties occurs in another way.

For instance, when one part such as a hand is covered, the simultaneous appearance of the two forms of the gross object—the covered and the uncovered—makes known its conjunction with two contradictory properties. Nor can it be said that this object consists solely of an uncovered form; for if even half were covered, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of seeing it as before, since its perception depends upon the perception of its parts, and if those parts are not seen, it would not be seen. If you argue that it is simply not seen [in that state], then let it be simply not seen; it cannot possess both being seen and not being seen simultaneously.
"Oṃ!

But surely there is indeed the perception of the whole even when its parts are concealed; so what is this undesirable consequence? If that were so, then the gross object would be perceived as it was before.
To this, someone here says:
Furthermore, the contact of the sense organ with the whole (avayavin) is the cause for the perception of grossness, being assisted by the contact of the sense organ with the many parts;
however, when half is obstructed, there is no contact of the sense organ with the majority of the parts,
and therefore there is no apprehension of grossness.
He too should be asked thus:

Is that which is called "gross" something other than the whole (*avayavin*), or is it the very same [whole] that is gross by virtue of pervading many [parts]? In that regard, if the whole itself is the gross [object], then one must consider how it is that the grossness is not perceived when that [whole] is perceived. Or, if you say that "grossness" is a specific dimension (*parimāṇa*) which is a quality (*guṇa*) and is indeed distinct from the substance (*dravya*), then in that case, this substance would be perceived as being devoid of dimension.
However, it cannot be associated with one size after another,
nor is the postulation of multiple sizes for it even tenable, because all of them are not perceived simultaneously; furthermore,
the cessation of the perception of a perceptible object is not logical.
That very substance is the object of that vision.

If it is argued that "it is the dimension of the part itself that is perceived," then in that case, let that very part, as connected with its own dimension, be what is directly perceived at the time of obscuration; the whole would not exist.
If you say, "Due to the cause of error—namely, inherence in the same object—the whole itself appears as if connected with the dimension of the part," that too is not tenable.
There would be the undesirable consequence of both the part and the whole appearing with equal dimensions;
for that large part which possesses that dimension appears as connected with its own dimension,
and if one accepts the appearance of the whole as being connected with that same dimension, it follows that both the part and the whole appear with equal dimensions.
If it is argued that the aforementioned appearance does not exist as something devoid of magnitude, because that part appears [as such], then this might be the case:
that part which the whole is connected with and appears to have a certain magnitude appears by abandoning its own [inherent] magnitude.
Furthermore, it is impossible to postulate this [magnitude] because a part devoid of magnitude is never perceived;
moreover, due to the cause of error— namely, inherence in the same object— an aggregate might appear as possessing the magnitude of even fewer parts,
yet an error cannot be established without a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*).
Let it be then that only a gross part is perceived.

In that case, just as during the state of being covered, let even a grosser part be perceived during the state of being uncovered; for if there were no sensory contact with the parts situated in between, the perception of a gross whole consisting of the most [numerous] parts would be impossible.
It might be argued that the perception of all parts is not the cause of the perception of a gross object, but rather the perception of many parts.
Even this [argument] is not correct;
for when one stands facing a mountain or the like, the perception of its grossness is not as it is when one sees the nearer parts from positions situated in front, behind, or in between.

Therefore, as long as there is no perception of every single part without exception, how could there be a cognition of the most gross object? Furthermore, parts situated in the front, back, and middle are not perceived simultaneously;

so how could the whole (*avayavin*) be seen as gross? If it is argued that the gross whole is perceived when the parts of the various directions are perceived in succession, then one must consider what exactly is being perceived at other times.

If it is argued that [the object] consists of parts (*avayava*), then since even those parts situated between the front and the middle are not perceived simultaneously, how could that [composite] also be perceptible? Thus, neither the composite whole nor its parts are perceptible; consequently, nothing at all would be seen.
Therefore, it is established that the appearance of a gross object as having both covered and uncovered forms is indeed a manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).
In the same way, a contradiction between the colored and the colorless is to be expected;
for when a single gross object is perceived simultaneously as having both a colored and a colorless form, it reveals its own possession of two contradictory forms.
[Objection: But surely only the part is colored, while the whole (avayavin) is of a single, colorless form.
If this were so, then when one part is red, the whole would be seen as having a non-red form;
but such is not the case.
Alternatively, redness is indeed the conjunction with a coloring substance.

Furthermore, when a part is in conjunction with a coloring substance, the whole must also be [colored] by it; for according to the established rule, that which is the effect must necessarily be conjoined with that which is conjoined with its cause.
To this, someone says: "The whole is indeed colored."
For indeed, when a portion of a cloth is dyed with saffron, there arises the cognition "the cloth is dyed with saffron";

therefore, the whole (avayavin) must be conjoined with the dyeing substance. Consequently, that whole would likewise not manifest any other color, because the dyeing substance, by coming into close proximity, conceals the object's own form.
Furthermore, a substance connects with its own form;

for example, a dyed part, whose innate form has been concealed, appears as connected with the form inherent in the dyeing substance. In that case, it would follow—indeed, it is unavoidable—that even in the whole (the cloth) which is in conjunction with the dyeing substance, no other color would be perceived.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the whole (avayavin) is colored [only in part];
however, another [author] resolves this by means of the non-pervasive occurrence (avyāpyavṛtti) of conjunction (saṃyoga), for he says: "Conjunction occurs non-pervasively, just like sound."
Therefore, that which is both colored and colorless has the same meaning;

it must be questioned in this way: how can it be non-pervasive? For if it were inherent in its own substratum like color and so forth, it would indeed be pervasive; or if it were not inherent, it would simply not exist there, like fragrance in insubstantial things.
If you argue that its existence and non-existence in a single locus constitute a non-pervasive occurrence, such might be the case.
Just as even contradictory qualities such as color and taste may reside in a single substratum, so too might existence and non-existence of conjunction occur simultaneously in one and the same place;
alas, what a manifestation of delusion this is!

For non-existence (*abhāva*) has the nature of the cessation of existence (*bhāvanivṛtti*); no other form of it is observed apart from this cessation of existence. And how could that which has the nature of the cessation of something exist while that very thing is present? Or, if it did exist, it would abandon its nature as the cessation of that thing. To illustrate: even one who sees fire might proceed toward it if seeking water, because he sees fire as distinct from water; thus, the absence of water is established [by that sight]. If you argue that there is no proceeding [toward the fire] because the absence of water is established through non-perception (*anupalambha*), we reply: let the absence of water be established through non-perception; nevertheless, one who seeks water would still proceed [toward the fire] if he were to imagine the presence of water.

Now, if there were water there, it would be perceived; what follows from this? If one argues that the non-existence of water is established simply because of its non-perception, then although the proof of the absence of water is indeed accepted, nevertheless, for one who desires that water, there might still be an inclination toward action based on the suspicion that it might exist.

Since existence and non-existence of conjunction are observed simultaneously in one and the same place, we postulate it in this way rather than by our own whim. Now, is non-existence perceived as consisting of the negation of existence, or otherwise? In that case, if non-existence is established as having the form of the cessation of existence, how could the perception of existence not be erroneous? Furthermore, non-existence cannot consist of the non-negation of existence.
It would be a mere name, yet the existence of an object does not follow from its being a mere name.
Furthermore, since color and taste do not exclude one another, how could the term "color" serve as an example here? Nor do we accept the inherence of color and taste in a single substrate.
Sound, likewise, is unestablished as being non-pervasive; how then could it be postulated for the purpose of removing the doubt at hand? Enough of this excessive talk.

Alternatively, the gross object is perceived as occupying both that space and a non-that space; and between these two—occupying that space and occupying a non-that space—there exists a contradiction based on their mutual non-existence being inseparable.
Therefore, there is a conjunction of contradictory properties in the gross object.
Regarding that location:
it might be argued as follows.

How is it that there is no deviation from the mutual absence [of one thing] in the two locations—this and that? It is said: here, when one location is being delimited, its loss of that nature (tādrūpya) is excluded; for if that were not excluded, it would follow that there is no delimitation of it at all. And just as the loss [of nature] is excluded, so too is the other location, which possesses that loss, excluded. For if the location being delimited were of the same nature as the other location, then it would be perceived as having precisely that form.
However, when a location manifests in its own form, excluding the form of another location, it is determined to be unconnected with that other location.
And just as a location is unconnected with another location, so too the form pervaded by that location which serves as its substratum becomes delimited by the non-contact with other locations;
for how could a form pervaded by one location exist in another location where it is absent? Just as a jar pervaded by one location does not exist in another location?
Is it uninterrupted (*avicchinna*) or interrupted (*vicchinna*)?

If you argue that there is no occurrence [of the form] in another location because it is not perceived there, how can its absence in a distant other location be established? Therefore, even one who does not wish to admit it must say this: namely, that a form which pervades one location does not exist in another location; for if it did, it would follow that it must pervade that other location as well, since it would be existing there while being devoid of that [other] location.
Nor can its pervasion (vyāpti) be ascertained, because other parts are impossible;

by this, that which someone has said is refuted—namely, "just as a single entity, producing [effects] in those places and not those places, is not contradictory"—for that too is not consistent with the present context.
For it is only existence and non-existence that are contradictory by way of mutual exclusion, not two entities (vastu).
The contradiction between two entities, however, consists in their non-deviation from mutual non-existence;
therefore, whatever entity is characterized by the exclusion of another entity, that very entity is indeed contradictory to it.
Om. R.

Furthermore, the capacity to produce one effect does not invariably entail the absence of the capacity for other effects; for it is the non-perception of a thing that establishes its invariable concomitance with the absence of another thing. Since the capacity to produce other effects is also determined when a form possessing the capacity to produce one effect is perceived, how can there be an absence of that [other] capacity? However, a form connected to one location, being perceived as excluding a form associated with another location, is contradictory to the presence of that [other] location and thus invariably concomitant with its absence.

Just as in the case of two objects that are extremely similar and perceived simultaneously, where— despite a difference in form— their distinction is not discerned from a distance, one establishes their difference by relying on a contradiction determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is caused solely by the difference in location;
for it is impossible to conceive of existence and contradiction coexisting when there is no difference in form.

As for the one who says— relying on direct perception— that just as a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) operates across distinct [senses] such as the eyes and so forth because its production is dependent upon them, so too another [consciousness] existing in different locations will not be divided; even he, while positing a contradiction based on the difference in location, fails to demonstrate his own proficiency by attributing a contradiction in the entity itself to a difference in its causes,
for consciousness has no location whatsoever, being immaterial (*amūrta*).
Regarding "local occurrence" (*deśavṛtti*):
it might be argued that just as there is contradiction caused by a difference in location, so too there could be contradiction caused by a difference in cause.
For what actual distinction is there between a difference in cause and a difference in location?
It has been stated here that the contradiction between entities is caused by their non-deviation from mutual non-existence (*parasparābhāvāvyabhicāra*).
That [distinction] resides in the difference of location, not in the difference of cause;

for when two forms possessing different locations are perceived through mutual exclusion, they are invariably concomitant with the absence of one another, but this is not the case when there is a difference of cause even if there is a difference of location.

Thus, having established the presence of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*) regarding the composite whole—based on the existence or non-existence of the states of trembling, color, and obscuration, and based on the distinction of location as the fourth factor—the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) of the reason is now proven;
it remains only for its pervasion (*vyāpti*) with its own probandum to be demonstrated.

For in this world, the conventional usage of non-difference among things is observed to be based solely on the absence of the association of contradictory properties, since no other cause is possible and no other cause is perceived.
Therefore, if a conventional usage of non-difference were to occur even when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties, it would abandon its pervading cause, namely "being a cause.
Consequently, by the non-perception of that pervader, [the usage] is excluded from that [cause] and is thereby pervaded by the absence of contradictory properties;
and the conjunction of contradictory properties is the opposite of that [absence].

Therefore, this is the stage of the perception of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*); [it concerns] the state of possessing a cause (*nimittavattva*). Therefore, the pervasion... [omitted in R].

Thus, when its threefold nature has been established in this way, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) find no opportunity; indeed,
when these thorns of refutation fabricated by many of evil intellect have been thus extracted by me.
This very path of the Teacher’s doctrine has been purified by him;
let people proceed by casting aside envy.
Thus ends this refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*).
